title: What must employers in Japan do to prevent heatstroke at work?
description: Japan's heatstroke rule in force since June 1, 2025: Article 612-2 reporting systems, response procedures, informing workers, training, and penalties.
shortAnswer: Since June 1, 2025, Article 612-2 of Japan's Ordinance on Industrial Safety and Health, added by MHLW Ordinance No. 57 of 2025, requires employers to set up a system for reporting suspected heatstroke and written, workplace specific response procedures before any work with a heatstroke risk, and to make both known to everyone doing it. Covered work is at WBGT 28 or above, or 31°C or above, for an hour or more continuously or over four hours a day.
keyTakeaways: MHLW Ordinance No. 57 of 2025, promulgated on April 15, 2025 and in force from June 1, 2025, added Article 612-2 to the Ordinance on Industrial Safety and Health. It is made under the Industrial Safety and Health Act.

Three things are mandatory before covered work starts: a reporting system for suspected heatstroke, written procedures for each workplace covering removal from work, cooling and medical care, and informing the people doing the work about both.

The MHLW circular of May 20, 2025 defines covered work as work in a place at WBGT 28 or above or 31°C or above, expected to last an hour or more continuously or more than four hours a day. It covers non-employees working at the same place.

Training is not named in Article 612-2, but the circular says first aid for suspected heatstroke belongs in the safety and health education required at hiring and for supervisors, and the MHLW basic guideline calls for advance health education for managers and workers.

Breach of the measures the ordinance requires can be prosecuted under Article 119 of the Act: imprisonment of up to six months or a fine of up to 500,000 yen, with the fine also imposed on the employer under Article 122.
regulator: Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW), through Prefectural Labor Bureaus and Labor Standards Inspection Offices
appliesTo: All employers in Japan whose work involves continuous or prolonged work in hot conditions, indoors or outdoors
Principal contractors and every subcontractor at mixed work sites such as construction sites
Workers and non-employees, such as self-employed contractors, who do covered work at the same place
Site managers, supervisors (shokuchō) and safety and health staff who receive reports and run the procedures

sections.heading: Which rule requires heatstroke measures in Japan?

blocks.text: The requirement is Article 612-2 of the Ordinance on Industrial Safety and Health (労働安全衛生規則, Ministry of Labour Ordinance No. 32 of 1972), in the chapter on temperature and humidity. It was added by [MHLW Ordinance No. 57 of 2025](https://www.mhlw.go.jp/content/001476790.pdf), made under Article 27(1) of the Industrial Safety and Health Act (Act No. 57 of 1972), promulgated on April 15, 2025, and in force from June 1, 2025.

The detail of how the rule operates is in an enforcement circular from the Director General of the Labour Standards Bureau to the Prefectural Labor Bureaus (Kihatsu 0520 No. 6, May 20, 2025), published by the [Kagoshima Labor Bureau](https://jsite.mhlw.go.jp/kagoshima-roudoukyoku/content/contents/2025-0529-9_1.pdf). The circular states that the new article is based on Article 22 of the Act and places a duty on each individual employer.

The circular explains why the rule was made. Heatstroke (熱中症, netchūshō) caused 1,195 deaths and injuries requiring four or more days off work in 2024, the highest since records began, and deaths had exceeded 30 for three years in a row, about 4% of all occupational deaths. Most fatal cases involved early symptoms being left unattended or a delayed response, so the rule targets early detection and fast response rather than prevention in general.

blocks.title: Wording change from October 1, 2026
blocks.text: As at November 2026, the [e-Gov text of the ordinance](https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/law/347M50002000032) shows Article 612-2 restated from October 1, 2026 by MHLW Ordinance No. 116 of 2026, which accompanies amendments to the Industrial Safety and Health Act. The article now uses the defined term "work engagers" (sagyō jūjisha) for the people who must be able to report and be informed. This matches the circular's position since 2025 that non-employees doing the work at the same place are covered.

sections.heading: Which work does the heatstroke rule cover?

blocks.text: The rule covers work in a hot place that is expected to last an hour or more continuously, or more than four hours in a day. The circular defines a hot place as one where the wet bulb globe temperature (WBGT) is 28 or above or the air temperature is 31°C or above.

items: **Not only fixed sites.** A hot place can include a business trip destination, work across several locations, and travel between work locations.
**Non-routine work counts.** Temporary and non-routine work is covered if it is expected to meet the conditions.

**How to judge the conditions.** In principle WBGT or temperature should be measured where the work happens. For well ventilated outdoor work, weather forecasts, including smartphone apps, or the Ministry of the Environment's heat illness prevention information site may be used instead.
**Below the threshold.** Where work is not covered, employers should still endeavor to apply equivalent measures, because work intensity and clothing can raise the risk.
**Who is protected.** The people doing the work include non-employees working at the same place as employees, not only the employer's own workers.

blocks.text: At mixed work sites, such as construction sites where several businesses work in the same place, the duty applies to the principal contractor and to every subcontractor. The circular states that if the measures are missing, every business at the site is in breach, not only the principal contractor. It suggests the businesses jointly set one emergency contact and post it where everyone can see it.

sections.heading: What must employers put in place?

blocks.text: Before covered work begins, the employer must have a reporting system, written response procedures for each workplace, and evidence that the people doing the work know both. Article 612-2(1) covers reporting and Article 612-2(2) covers the procedures.

items: **Reporting system (Article 612-2(1)).** Set and display the contact details of the person who receives reports, such as the site manager, and how to reach them, so reports can be made at any time during the work. A report must be possible both when a person has symptoms themselves and when someone notices symptoms in a coworker. The circular recommends active detection as well: patrols by the responsible person, a buddy system in which two or more workers check each other, wearable devices combined with other methods, and regular two way contact.

**Response procedures (Article 612-2(2)).** For each workplace, set the measures to stop symptoms getting worse and the procedure for carrying them out, including removal from the work, cooling the body, and a medical examination or treatment where needed. The circular gives cooling examples (removing work clothes and pouring water, ice baths, a cool rest area, mist fans, ice slurry drinks) and says the person should not be left alone because their condition can change suddenly.

**Informing (both paragraphs).** Make the reporting system and the procedures known to the people doing the work. Posting in a visible place, email, documents and oral briefings such as morning meetings are all acceptable, but the circular says to combine methods where content is complex or some people miss the briefing.

blocks.text: The system and procedures must be in place before the first day of covered work, and for predictable summer outdoor work employers should prepare with time to spare. If the same people do the work continuously and have already been informed, the steps do not need repeating every day. The circular also recommends that procedures include the emergency contact network and the name and address of the receiving hospital, a plan for symptoms that worsen after the person goes home, and use of the #7119 emergency advice line when unsure.

blocks.title: Records are not required, but expect to be asked
blocks.text: The circular states that the ordinance does not require a record of how the information was communicated, but that employers must be able to respond appropriately when a Labor Standards Inspection Office checks. A dated record of what was posted, sent and briefed is the practical answer.

Article 612-2 requires informing rather than training, but two other instruments make heatstroke content part of required education. First, the circular states that where covered work is done, the safety and health education at hiring under Article 59(1) of the Act and the education for supervisors (shokuchō) under Article 60 include emergency measures, and that these include first aid for a person suspected of heatstroke, covering the new rule. The [Industrial Safety and Health Act training page](/regulations/japan-industrial-safety-and-health-act-training) explains those education duties.

Second, the MHLW Basic Guideline for Preventing Heatstroke in the Workplace (Kihatsu 0420 No. 3 of 2021, as revised on May 20, 2025 and attached to the circular) says that where workers work in hot and humid places, health education must be given in advance to the people managing the work and to the workers on four topics: heatstroke symptoms, prevention methods, emergency first aid, and case examples. The guideline also describes heat acclimatization over seven days or more for people new to hot work.

sections.heading: What are the penalties for not complying?

blocks.text: Because Article 612-2 implements Article 22 of the Industrial Safety and Health Act, failing to take the measures can be prosecuted under Article 119, which applies to breaches of Articles 20 to 25. As at November 2026, the [e-Gov text of the Act](https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/law/347AC0000000057) sets the penalty at imprisonment (kōkinkei) of up to six months or a fine of up to 500,000 yen for the person who committed the breach, and Article 122 imposes the same fine on the corporation or individual employer.

In practice, Labor Standards Inspection Offices check the rule during inspections and can require correction. The circular's statement that every business at a mixed site is in breach if the measures are missing means subcontractors cannot rely on the principal contractor.

sections.heading: How do you evidence heatstroke prevention?

blocks.text: Keep a record that ties each covered work activity to the three required measures and the education behind them.

items: A list of work activities assessed as covered, with the WBGT or temperature basis and expected duration.
The reporting contact sheet for each workplace, with the date it was posted or sent.
The written response procedures for each workplace, including emergency contacts and the receiving hospital.
Records showing who was informed and how, including non-employees and subcontractor staff.
Hiring and supervisor education records that list heatstroke first aid as a topic.
Pre-season health education records and an acclimatization plan for new starters.
A dated review of the procedures each year before the hot season, and after any incident.

blocks.text: For record structure, see [preparing training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit). Groups operating in several countries can compare this rule with [OSHA training requirements](/regulations/osha-training-requirements) and the [EU framework directive on safety and health training](/regulations/eu-osh-framework-directive-training).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry models Article 612-2, the related hiring and supervisor education duties, and the Basic Guideline topics as linked obligations, each with an audience, learning outcomes and an assessment point. Because the article was restated on October 1, 2026, both versions are held as dated obligations so materials citing the 2025 wording can be identified and checked.

faqs.q: Does the heatstroke rule apply to indoor work in Japan?
faqs.a: Yes. The rule applies wherever covered work takes place, indoors or outdoors. The circular also confirms that an indoor workplace where covered work is done is a hot workplace for the existing temperature control duty in Article 606 of the ordinance. Factories, kitchens and warehouses can all be covered if the WBGT or temperature and duration conditions are met.

faqs.q: Are subcontractors and self-employed workers covered?
faqs.a: Yes. The circular states that the people doing the work include non-employees working at the same place as employees, and that at mixed sites the principal contractor and every subcontractor carry the duty. Since October 1, 2026 the article itself uses the defined term work engagers. A joint emergency contact posted at the site is one suggested method.

faqs.q: Do we need to measure WBGT on site?
faqs.a: In principle, yes. The circular says whether a place is hot should be judged by measuring WBGT or temperature where the work happens. For well ventilated outdoor work, weather forecasts, including smartphone apps, or the Ministry of the Environment's heat illness prevention information site may be used instead.

faqs.q: Must employers keep records of heatstroke briefings?
faqs.a: The ordinance does not require a record of how the reporting system and procedures were communicated. The circular adds that employers must be able to respond appropriately when the Labor Standards Inspection Office checks, so a dated record of postings, emails and briefings is the practical way to show the rule was followed.
